DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
# Review: Menu Pricing Review, Spring 2026 (The Copper Kettle)

**What the author claims:**
- The proposals rest on till data, a competitor price check and the latest supplier information.
- The price rises keep each dish below the competitor midpoint.
- The rises add £810 a week, about £42,000 a year, and lift the main-course margin to about 71%.
- The mushroom risotto has the weakest margin and the lowest sales, so replacing it is an easy improvement.

**Bottom line:** the price rises themselves are reasonable and well positioned against competitors. But the paper's two main conclusions are contradicted by its own figures:
- **The risotto has the *highest* margin on the menu (80%), not the weakest.** Replacing it with a special at the specials' average margin (64%) would *lose* gross profit.
- **The £42,000 projection leaves out the 12% beef price rise reported in Section 4.** Allowing for it, the gain is about **£27,500 a year**, and the main-course margin stays roughly **flat at about 69%** rather than rising to 71%.

Taken together, the two proposals add about £17,000 a year, not £42,000, and the margin falls slightly. The price rises are worth doing; dropping the risotto isn't.

## What checks out

| Check | Calculation | Document |
|---|---|---|
| Margins | e.g. (16.50 − 5.10) / 16.50 | 69% / 72% / 75% / 60% / 80% ✓ |
| Weekly gain before beef costs | 310 × £1 + 260 × £1 + 120 × £2 | £810 ✓ |
| Annual | £810 × 52 | £42,120 ✓ |
| Competitor midpoints | fish £17.98, burger £16.50, steak £29.50 | all proposed prices below ✓ |

---

## 1. The risotto is the most profitable dish per pound of sales

From Table 1:

| Dish | Margin | Gross profit per plate | Weekly gross profit |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Mushroom risotto** | **80%** (highest) | £11.20 | £1,008 |
| Chicken curry | 75% | £10.90 | £1,962 |
| Beef burger | 72% | £10.80 | £2,808 |
| Fish and chips | 69% | £11.40 | £3,534 |
| Sirloin steak | **60%** (lowest) | £15.60 | £1,872 |

The weakest margin belongs to the **steak**, not the risotto. The risotto's sales are the lowest, but only joint lowest with specials (90 plates each).

**Replacing it is likely to lose money.** If the new special matches the specials' average 64% margin at the same £14 price, gross profit drops by about **£200 a week, roughly £10,500 a year**.

**It may also be the main vegetarian option.** If so, removing it could affect whole groups: a table may go elsewhere if one diner can't find a dish they want.

**Recommendation:** keep the risotto. If the menu needs a seasonal vegetarian dish, add one alongside it.

## 2. The projection leaves out the beef price rise

Section 4 reports a **12% rise in beef prices from 1 April**, the same day the new prices take effect. Section 5.3 doesn't include it:

| | Burger | Steak |
|---|---|---|
| Food cost now | £4.20 | £10.40 |
| After +12% | £4.70 | £11.65 |
| Extra cost per week | 260 × £0.50 = £131 | 120 × £1.25 = £150 |

- **Corrected gain:** £810 − £281 = **£529 a week, about £27,500 a year.**
- **The steak's margin falls further,** from 60% to about **58%**, even at £28. The burger's falls from 72% to about 71%. The steak price rise doesn't keep up with its cost rise in percentage terms.

## 3. The main-course margin doesn't rise to 71%

Taking all main courses together, and assuming specials average about £15 a plate:

| Scenario | Main-course margin |
|---|---|
| Now | ~69.4% |
| Price rises, ignoring beef (the paper's figures) | ~70.8%, the paper's "about 71%" |
| **Price rises with the beef increase** | **~69.2%** |
| **Plus replacing the risotto with a 64% special** | **~68.1%** |

Once the beef cost is included, the extra revenue earns a lower margin than the menu average. So the overall percentage barely moves, and it falls slightly if the risotto goes.

## 4. "Volumes will hold" is assumed, not tested

The paper bases this on competitive pricing and a loyal customer base. A small fall in volume is enough to cancel the gain:

| Dish | Volume loss that cancels the price rise (after beef costs) |
|---|---|
| Fish and chips | ~8% |
| Beef burger | ~9% |
| Sirloin steak | ~12% |

**The paper's evidence on this:**
- **Value position.** After the rises, The Copper Kettle is **no longer the cheapest** for any of the three dishes. Each new price is above the lowest competitor (£16.95, £15.50 and £27.00). The prices are still below the midpoints, so the paper's competitive claim holds, but the author's "remain the value option" goes too far.
- **Lunch trade.** Section 7 says weekday lunch, the most price-sensitive trade, is a small share of sales. But Friday and Saturday dinner make up "just under half", so the rest, including all lunches, is over half. The paper gives no figure to support "small".
- **The 2024 price change.** "No visible effect" is an impression, not a measured result.

## 5. Comparing April–May with January–February will mislead

Section 6 plans to compare the first eight weeks against January–February. For most restaurants, January and February are the quietest months of the year, so April–May volumes may well look *higher* even if the price rise drove some customers away.

**Fix:** compare with April–May 2025, or with booking numbers, so seasonal changes aren't mistaken for the effect of the price rise.

## 6. Smaller points

- **Trading days.** The Recommendation refers to "six trading days a week". Section 2 says Wednesday to Sunday, which is five. The annual figures use weekly totals, so they aren't affected, but the text should be corrected.
- **Steak pricing.** Even £29.50 would still be below the competitor midpoint. A larger steak rise, for example to £29, is worth considering given the beef cost increase: it would hold the steak's margin at about 60%.
- **Purpose versus scope.** The stated aim is to restore a 70% overall food margin. Main courses alone, at about 69%, can't get there through these changes. Starters, desserts and portion costs need reviewing too.

---

## What is sound

- **The price positioning.** All three new prices are below the competitor midpoints, as the author says. They're modest rises after 18 months without an increase.
- **The data.** Using two months of till data and current supplier information is the right basis, and every figure in Table 1 is internally consistent.
- **Monitoring by dish** is right, once the comparison period is fixed.

## Settled and open

**Settled by the paper's own figures:**
- The risotto has the highest margin on the menu, not the weakest.
- After the beef rise, the price changes add about £27,500 a year, not £42,000.
- The main-course margin stays at about 69%, and falls if the risotto is replaced.
- After the rises, the restaurant is no longer the cheapest of the group for these dishes.

**Open:**

| Question | What would settle it |
|---|---|
| Will volumes hold? | Year-on-year comparison of weekly dish sales from April |
| How price-sensitive is lunch trade? | Till data split by lunch and dinner |
| What margin would a seasonal vegetarian special earn? | A costed recipe |
| Is the risotto the main vegetarian choice for groups? | Till data on tables ordering it |

## Recommendation

**Approve the price rises,** with the projection restated at about £27,500 a year, and consider a larger rise on steak. **Don't approve removing the risotto.** Change the monitoring to compare with last year rather than January–February, and correct the reference to six trading days.
